title: Credit Spreads and Business Cycle Fluctuations
datasets: Federal Reserve H.15 Selected Interest Rates
research_question: Do bond-level, duration-matched corporate credit spreads forecast future US real activity beyond the term spread and policy rate, and does that forecasting power reflect default risk or a separate, time-varying excess bond premium tied to financial-intermediary risk-bearing capacity?
main_finding: The GZ credit spread substantially outperforms the Baa-Aaa and paper-bill spreads as a predictor of employment, industrial production and GDP growth; most of this predictive power, especially after 1985, comes from the excess bond premium rather than measured default risk, and orthogonalized shocks to the premium produce sizeable, persistent declines in consumption, investment, output and equity prices in a VAR.
research_gaps: Sample restricted to large, bond-market-active firms; bank-dependent firms untested
Causal, credit-supply interpretation of excess-bond-premium shocks relies on a standard but unverified recursive VAR ordering
No out-of-sample / real-time forecast evaluation is reported
Cannot cleanly separate the risk-bearing-capacity channel from a time-varying disaster-risk alternative
research_ideas: Construct an excess bank-loan premium from syndicated loan pricing data to test the mechanism among bank-dependent firms
Extend the excess bond premium to a growth-at-risk, quantile-regression framework
High-frequency identification of excess-bond-premium shocks around bank-capital and regulatory announcements
Construct a euro-area analogue of the GZ spread to test the mechanism against the sovereign-bank nexus
Use option-implied disaster-risk measures to separate the risk-bearing-capacity channel from time-varying disaster risk
